telephonitis, of telephone mania in all varieties. The chief of such new applications undoubtedly will be two—first, wireless telephony, filling the whole air of the world, once named free, with phantom voices of persons wirelessly telephoning to one another.

Most inventions give us for one atom of convenience forty ton of boredom and nuisance. So the wireless telephone, filling our lives with din, will, we anticipate, constitute the great Progress of the after-war period of advance towards goodness knows what next. Then for the second invention. That already announces itself as the transmutation of sounds into sights, as the making visible, in crude transparencies, of all the innumerable crashes and clangours of modern mechanism. An ingenious Professor, pioneer of Progress, has we learn already elaborated the appliances; and, one step on, we shall find ourselves at the great day of seeing by telephone, of seeing our friends at a distance, and indeed of seeing everything and everybody all together, just as we soon hope to hear them in our houses simultaneously. Thus life will, in the finally perfected Telephone Period, be a delightfully amusing jumble of sounds and sights, highly progressive, and likely to eliminate the unfit, or the peaceful. Those who have an obsolete craving for privacy had better therefore go to the front now. You never know what they may invent next. Progress is a terrible business. W. M.

The concentration of the Tochi column is now taking place and busy scenes are to be witnessed at Bannu and beyond.

The wall up $Tochi valley has not been doubled for Motor or Animal Transport like the one through the Khyber and in consequence there is great congestion in $ sections of it due to conveys of Animals and of Motor Vans which are accumulating supplies at the advanced base at MIRAN SHAH.
The lower sections of the road (as far as IDAK) is worked by animal conveys in stages, so as to minimises the transport of their food, while the upper section is supplied by Motor (Food Vans).

Some of the Animal conveys are 7 to 8 miles long: in addition to pickets on the heights throughout the whole length of the route the conveys are guarded by batches of troops marching with it, at the head and rear and at intervals along the column.
Convoy duty is not popular with the troops as the rate of progress is slow and the dust can be imagined.
Ballions marching up to the concentration centre are used for the purpose as far as possible.
Occasionally a returning column consisting of empty animals met with coming in the opposite direction and the road is so narrow that there is hardly room for both.
The road in consequence became blocked wherever a check occurs: camels occupy both the edges of the road and the centre is filled with pack mules, perhaps 6 abreast.
A refractory or team also causes exasperating delays as yoke when the animals get twisted in the $ considerable
persuasion are required to lead them in the right direction again: meanwhile nothing can pass.
The conveys are looking up into sections: long strings of Camels are followed by pack Mules, which in turn are succeeded by carts, drawn by pairs of mules or ponies.
The March Discipline is good considering all the circumstances, as many of the drivers are new to the work and the beasts themselves are not particularly answerable.
The difficulty of keeping Camels to the side of the road or of guiding draught $^{6}$ oxen can only be appreciated by those who have had to wait patiently for an opportunity to get pass.
The Camel men are of the picturesque figures and they have collected from all parts of the N.W. Frontier Province.
Some are patriarchal in appearance, others villianous to a degree.
Here and there one can be seen leading his string of 5 slouching animals with a huge woolcap in his hand from which he takes occasional pulls.
Others carry fearsome swords across their shoulders apparently to indicate which courage they could muster in case of attack.
Each Camel is fed by the nose to the tail of the one in pmol: they are unaccustomed to Motor traffic and occasionally stampside to the side of the road.
They are very clumsy in megothalaming obstacles and stumble over rocks or piles of road waste metal, shooting off their loads to one side.
Or one will break loose and tumble on in front of the car for considerable distance before it can be "shoed" into line again.
These convoys are hole to sudden attack at any point along the road.
On Oct 22nd, a party of 500 or 600 Mebgrads eluded the picked posts and crept along the Mullahs till within short range of the road.
The spot was very cleverly chosen and the leading animals were shot as they reached a culvert which gave the range.
The road soon became blocked and the drivers made for the nearest cover leaving the animals panic stricken, so that the confusion can be imagined.
The convoy guard of 120 men returned the enemy's fire, but the latter were on both sides of the road and cleverly concealed.
It was only in the event of 3 armoured cars and 50 Fuel Vans filled with reinforcements that the road could be cleared of dead and wounded animals and any progress could be made.
Eventually after a stubborn fight of 6 hours the enemy was driven off and the convoy extricated.
Mountain Guns from a neighbouring height took part in this action, as well as an aeroplane which machine - gunned the enemy's tangars and dropped bombs into the Mullahs.
As each bomb dropped the Maashsuds were heard to cheer and beat tom - toms.

Some 20 or 30 loads from dead and wounded animals had to be abandoned in the road and these were looked when night fell, but they counted chiefly of cement and thus - too heavy for removal over into which the hills pit. when the raiders had to retreat.
Our losses were about 20 men killed and wounded - including a very gallant medical officer who was to have been demobilized only two days later.
